options: WHOIS
Reverse DNS
Traceroute
Ping
questions.hint: Domain registration records.
questions.explanation: WHOIS retrieves registration information for domains and IP resources, such as registration dates and registrar details, where available.

questions.question: Which email authentication control lets a domain publish which mail servers may send email on its behalf?
options: DKIM
SPF
DMARC
TLS
questions.hint: It’s a list of permitted senders.
questions.explanation: SPF (Sender Policy Framework) publishes which servers are authorised to send for a domain. DKIM signs messages, and DMARC sets the policy using both.

questions.question: Which email authentication method uses a cryptographic signature to show a message wasn’t altered in transit?
options: SPF
DMARC
DKIM
POP3
questions.hint: Think ‘keys’ and signatures.
questions.explanation: DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) adds a cryptographic signature that the receiver checks with the domain’s public key to confirm authenticity and integrity.

questions.question: Which control tells receiving servers what to do with mail that fails SPF and DKIM checks?
options: SPF
DKIM
MX records
DMARC
questions.hint: It’s the policy layer on top of the other two.
questions.explanation: DMARC builds on SPF and DKIM and tells receivers how to handle failures: none, quarantine or reject. It also provides reporting.

questions.question: Which three actions can a DMARC policy request for mail that fails its checks?
options: None, quarantine or reject
Allow, warn or delete
Encrypt, sign or forward
Log, archive or bounce
questions.hint: One of them does nothing at all.
questions.explanation: DMARC policies are none (monitor only), quarantine (treat as suspicious, e.g. junk) or reject (refuse the message).

questions.question: What does ‘-all’ at the end of an SPF record mean?
options: Every server in the world may send for the domain
Mail from unauthorised servers should fail SPF (a hard fail)
SPF checking is turned off
Only DKIM-signed mail is accepted
questions.hint: The minus sign is strict.
questions.explanation: ‘-all’ is the SPF hard fail: mail from sources not listed in the policy should fail SPF validation.

questions.question: Which HTML element creates a hyperlink, and is worth inspecting in a suspicious email?
options: The tag
The <table> tag
The anchor tag <a>
The <style> tag
questions.hint: Hyperlinks use the href attribute.
questions.explanation: The anchor tag (<a href=…>) creates hyperlinks. The visible link text can differ from the real destination in the href, so analysts check both.

questions.question: An attachment is a harmless-looking PDF whose only purpose is to get you to click a malicious link inside it. What is it?
options: Macro malware
A tracking pixel
A recon email
A lure document
questions.hint: The file itself may contain no malware.
questions.explanation: A lure document isn’t necessarily malicious itself; it’s designed to persuade the recipient to click a malicious link or take another unsafe step.

questions.question: A phishing email uses a Bitly link. Why do attackers use URL shortening?
options: To hide the final destination behind a redirect
To make the page load faster for victims
To encrypt the link so filters can’t read it
To prove to the victim that the link is safe
questions.hint: You can’t see where it really goes.
questions.explanation: URL shorteners replace the real destination with a short link that redirects. It hides where the link goes, so analysts resolve the redirect safely before trusting it.

questions.question: Which HTTP status code means a resource has been permanently redirected?
questions.hint: It’s a 3xx code.
questions.explanation: HTTP 301 means ‘Moved Permanently’. The Location header in the response shows where the browser is being sent, which can reveal a shortened link’s target.

questions.question: When checking a redirect, which HTTP response header shows the destination URL?
options: User-Agent
Host
Location
Accept
questions.hint: It tells the browser where to go next.
questions.explanation: The Location header in a redirect response holds the destination URL. User-Agent and Host are request headers.

questions.question: What does the User-Agent header identify?
options: The organisation that owns the website
The final destination of a redirect
The user’s account name on the site
The browser or client making the web request
questions.hint: It’s sent by the client.
questions.explanation: User-Agent is a request header that identifies the browser, application or client making the request.

questions.question: Which HTTP status code means a request succeeded?
questions.hint: The ‘OK’ code.
questions.explanation: HTTP 200 OK means the request succeeded and the resource is available. 500 is an internal server error.

questions.question: A web capture of a phishing link returns HTTP 500. What does that mean?
options: The page has been permanently moved to a new address
The server hit an internal error and couldn’t fulfil the request
The request succeeded and the page loaded normally
The page requires the visitor to sign in first
questions.hint: 5xx codes are server-side problems.
questions.explanation: HTTP 500 Internal Server Error is a generic server-side error: the server couldn’t complete the request.

questions.question: Attackers send phishing from a real Gmail-style webmail account or host files on a well-known cloud service. What is this tactic called?
options: Typosquatting
Header spoofing
Legitimate service abuse
DNS blackholing
questions.hint: Trusted services help them blend in.
questions.explanation: Legitimate service abuse uses trusted webmail, marketing or cloud-hosting services to deliver phishing or host malicious files, so it’s harder to block.

questions.question: An attacker impersonates the CEO and pressures a finance assistant to make an urgent transfer. Which BEC pattern is this?
options: A vendor attack
Zombie phishing
A recon email
CEO fraud
questions.hint: The executive is the disguise.
questions.explanation: CEO fraud is a business email compromise where the attacker impersonates a senior executive to pressure staff into transferring money or taking another sensitive action.

questions.question: A supplier’s hijacked mailbox is used to send fake invoices to its customers. Which BEC scenario is this?
options: A vendor attack
CEO fraud
Whaling
Smishing
questions.hint: The compromised business is a supplier.
questions.explanation: In a vendor attack, a compromised or impersonated business account sends fraudulent payment requests or invoices to the people it does business with.

questions.question: An email asks a company to send all future payments to a new bank account. Which BEC scenario is this?
options: A recon email
An alternative payment attack
Credential stuffing
A tracking pixel attack
questions.hint: The payment destination changes.
questions.explanation: An alternative payment attack directs the victim to send future payments to an attacker-controlled account. A call-back to a known number defeats it.

questions.question: A compromised mailbox replies to an old, genuine email thread and slips in a malicious link. What is this called?
options: Whaling
Typosquatting
Zombie phishing
Spam recon
questions.hint: The old conversation comes back to life.
questions.explanation: Zombie phishing reuses a compromised mailbox to reply to old legitimate threads, taking advantage of the trust in an existing conversation.

questions.question: In a phishing investigation, what is an ‘artifact’?
options: A deleted email recovered from the company backups
The final written report sent to management
An antivirus signature created by the vendor
A specific piece of information collected from the email for analysis
questions.hint: Things you collect: addresses, URLs, hashes.
questions.explanation: An artifact is a specific piece of information from the email, such as a sending address, URL or file hash, collected for investigation, sharing or blocking.

questions.question: Which of these is a web artifact from a phishing email?
options: The full URL and its root domain
The sending server IP
The attachment’s SHA-256 hash
The Reply-To address
questions.hint: Web means links.
questions.explanation: Web artifacts are mainly the full URL and root domain. The sending IP and Reply-To are email artifacts, and hashes are file artifacts.

questions.question: Which set makes up the core file artifacts from a suspicious attachment?
options: Sender, subject and date
File name, extension and hash
Full URL and root domain
Received headers and Message-ID
questions.hint: Everything about the file itself.
questions.explanation: File artifacts are the attachment name, its extension and a cryptographic hash (preferably SHA-256) for reputation checks and blocking.

questions.question: Why do analysts record every recipient of a phishing email?
options: To send each of them a formal warning letter
To block all of their accounts as a precaution
To understand the scope of the campaign and who to notify
Because the recipients are usually the attackers
questions.hint: Who else might have clicked?
questions.explanation: Knowing everyone who received the email shows the campaign’s scope and lets you notify and protect them all.

questions.question: Why might attackers put targets in the BCC field?
options: To make the email pass SPF and DKIM checks
To encrypt the message for every recipient
To prove the email came from a real company
To hide recipients from each other in a mass phishing email
questions.hint: Blind carbon copy.
questions.explanation: BCC hides recipient addresses from other recipients, so a mass phishing email looks personal and no one sees how many others received it.

questions.question: Why is the sending server IP useful when investigating a phishing email?
options: It shows the server that actually sent it and can expose spoofing
It shows where the recipient was when they read it
It proves the email is safe if it’s a UK address
It lets the analyst decrypt the email’s body
questions.hint: The From address can lie; the server tells you more.
questions.explanation: The sending server IP identifies the machine that actually transmitted the message, which helps reveal the true origin and detect sender spoofing.

questions.question: What does a reverse DNS lookup do?
options: Maps a hostname to an IP address
Maps an IP address back to a hostname
Finds who registered a domain
Shows an email’s delivery route
questions.hint: It works backwards from the usual DNS lookup.
questions.explanation: Reverse DNS turns an IP address into a hostname, helping analysts see which provider or server actually sent an email.

questions.question: What is the root domain of https://login.example-bank.co.uk/verify?id=7?
options: login.example-bank.co.uk/verify
https://login
example-bank.co.uk
verify?id=7
questions.hint: The core domain, without the subdomain or path.
questions.explanation: The root domain is the core registered domain, example-bank.co.uk. The full URL includes the protocol, subdomain, path and query.

questions.question: Why do analysts collect a file hash from a suspicious attachment?
options: To open the file without any risk
To decrypt the file so it can be read
To find out exactly who sent the file
To identify the exact file and check its reputation
questions.hint: A fingerprint for the file.
questions.explanation: A hash is a fixed-length value calculated from the file’s data. It uniquely identifies that version of the file for reputation checks and blocking.

questions.question: Which hashing algorithm does the course treat as the current standard for file hashing?
options: SHA-256
MD5
SHA-1
Base64
questions.hint: The other two hashes have known collision weaknesses.
questions.explanation: SHA-256 is the current standard. MD5 and SHA-1 have known collision weaknesses, and Base64 isn’t a hash at all.

questions.question: What is a hash collision?
options: Two copies of a file with different hashes
Two different inputs producing the same hash
A hash that can’t be calculated
An encrypted file that won’t open
questions.hint: Why MD5 and SHA-1 aren’t trusted.
questions.explanation: A collision is when two different inputs produce the same hash value. Known collision weaknesses are why MD5 and SHA-1 shouldn’t be preferred.

questions.question: Which PowerShell cmdlet calculates a file’s hash, using SHA-256 by default?
options: Get-Content
Test-Path
Get-FileHash
Get-Process
questions.hint: It does exactly what its name says.
questions.explanation: Get-FileHash calculates a file hash and uses SHA-256 by default, though other algorithms can be specified.

questions.question: On Linux, which command produces a SHA-256 hash of a file?
options: md5sum
chmod
grep
sha256sum
questions.hint: It names its algorithm.
questions.explanation: sha256sum generates a SHA-256 hash. sha1sum and md5sum do the same for the older algorithms.

questions.question: Which file format stores a whole email, including headers and body, so it can be inspected in a text editor?
options: .eml
.csv
.exe
.png
questions.hint: E for email.
questions.explanation: An .eml file stores an email message with its headers and body. Outlook’s equivalent format is .msg.

questions.question: Where should an analyst open and investigate suspicious emails and websites?
options: On their normal work laptop, with care
On a dedicated dirty system or virtual machine
On the company’s main email server
On a colleague’s spare computer
questions.hint: Keep risky work away from production.
questions.explanation: A ‘dirty system’ is a dedicated non-production machine for risky tasks, so a malicious link or file can’t harm the corporate network.

questions.question: What does PhishTool do in a phishing investigation?
options: Sends simulated phishing emails to test staff awareness
Blocks malicious domains at the perimeter firewall
Automatically extracts email, web and file artifacts and helps produce a report
Encrypts suspicious emails so no one can open them
questions.hint: It speeds up artifact collection.
questions.explanation: PhishTool is a forensic email analysis platform that extracts artifacts automatically, tags indicators and generates investigation reports.

questions.question: An analyst wants to see what a phishing page looks like without visiting it. What should they use?
options: Their own browser, in a private window
A WHOIS lookup on the page’s domain
The DMARC aggregate report for the domain
A URL visualisation service like URL2PNG or urlscan.io
questions.hint: A screenshot taken somewhere else.
questions.explanation: URL visualisation tools render the page remotely and return a screenshot, so the analyst can inspect it without browsing to it directly.

questions.question: A URL and file hash both come back clean on VirusTotal. What should the analyst conclude?
options: It hasn’t been flagged yet, which doesn’t prove it’s safe
It is definitely safe and can be released
It must be a false positive from the user
It should be deleted without further checks
questions.hint: New and targeted attacks may not be known yet.
questions.explanation: A clean reputation result only means no vendor has flagged it yet. New or targeted attacks often aren’t detected at first, so other evidence still matters.

questions.question: Which public sources list known malicious and phishing URLs?
options: WHOIS and reverse DNS
URLhaus and PhishTank
SPF and DKIM
CyberChef and Wireshark
questions.hint: Community threat feeds.
questions.explanation: URLhaus is a public database of malicious URLs, and PhishTank is a community-verified list of phishing sites.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a reputation check and sandboxing?
options: Reputation runs the file; sandboxing looks it up in an online database
They are two names for the same automated scan
Reputation asks if others have flagged it; sandboxing runs it to watch what it does
Sandboxing only works on URLs; reputation only works on files
questions.hint: One looks it up; the other watches it.
questions.explanation: Reputation checks ask whether something has been seen and flagged before. Sandboxing executes it in isolation to observe its actual behaviour.

questions.question: Which online service detonates submitted files in cloud virtual machines and produces behavioural reports?
options: WHOIS
PhishTank
CyberChef
Hybrid Analysis
questions.hint: An online malware sandbox.
questions.explanation: Hybrid Analysis runs submitted files or URLs in cloud-based virtual machines and produces behavioural and reputation reports.

questions.question: A sandbox report shows malware reaching out to a remote server for instructions. What is that server called?
options: Command and control (C2)
A mail relay
A web proxy
A DNS sinkhole
questions.hint: Where the attacker gives orders from.
questions.explanation: Command and control (C2) infrastructure is what compromised systems contact to receive commands, send data or download more modules.

questions.question: What does a RAT give an attacker?
options: A list of the victim’s contacts only
Remote access and control of the victim’s system
A copy of the victim’s antivirus logs
Access to the victim’s SPF record
questions.hint: Remote Access Trojan.
questions.explanation: A Remote Access Trojan lets an attacker remotely access and control the infected system.

questions.question: What is the difference between a preventative and a reactive control?
options: Preventative is always technical; reactive is always staff training
Reactive controls are applied before an attack; preventative ones after
Preventative stops attacks before harm; reactive contains them after detection
There is no real difference; the terms are interchangeable
questions.hint: Before versus after.
questions.explanation: Preventative controls aim to stop or reduce attacks before harm occurs. Reactive controls are used after detection to contain the threat and limit impact.

questions.question: Security awareness training is an example of which type of control?
options: Technical
Physical
Reactive only
Administrative
questions.hint: It’s about people and process, not technology.
questions.explanation: Administrative controls are people- and process-based, like policies, procedures and training. Email filtering would be a technical control.

questions.question: Emails from outside the organisation are tagged [EXTERNAL]. What is the purpose?
options: To make users pause before clicking, opening or replying
To encrypt every email from outside the company
To block external email unless IT approves it
To prove the sender passed SPF and DKIM checks
questions.hint: It’s a visual warning.
questions.explanation: External email marking warns users that a message came from outside, so they think twice. It doesn’t authenticate the sender like SPF, DKIM and DMARC do.

questions.question: In Microsoft Exchange, what is used to automatically add an [EXTERNAL] tag to incoming mail?
options: A DKIM key
A mail flow rule
A reverse DNS record
A tracking pixel
questions.hint: A rule that acts when conditions are met.
questions.explanation: A mail flow rule automatically takes an action when conditions are met, such as marking messages that come from outside the organisation.

questions.question: A spam filter learns from messages users mark as spam or not spam. What type of filter is it?
options: A rule-based filter
A gateway filter
A Bayesian filter
A desktop filter
questions.hint: Statistical and adaptive.
questions.explanation: A Bayesian filter uses statistics learned from classified messages to judge future email. Rule-based filters apply fixed criteria instead.

questions.question: Where does a gateway spam filter sit?
options: On each individual user’s laptop or desktop
Inside the recipient’s web browser as an add-on
On the sending organisation’s mail server
At the organisation’s network or email gateway, before delivery
questions.hint: At the edge.
questions.explanation: A gateway spam filter inspects inbound mail at the organisation’s edge before delivery. Hosted filters run in the cloud, and desktop filters run on individual devices.

questions.question: What is the difference between attachment filtering and attachment sandboxing?
options: Filtering applies rules to block or strip files; sandboxing runs them in isolation to watch behaviour
Filtering runs the file to watch it; sandboxing simply deletes it straight away
Both only check the file name and ignore the contents completely
Sandboxing is done by the recipient; filtering is done by the sender
questions.hint: Rules versus running it.
questions.explanation: Attachment filtering uses rules like file type to block, strip or quarantine. Attachment sandboxing detonates the file in an isolated environment before delivery.

questions.question: Why do organisations run authorised simulated phishing campaigns?
options: To identify and discipline staff who click links
To measure whether staff spot, report or fall for phishing
To test how quickly the mail server delivers email
To collect staff passwords for a security audit
questions.hint: Testing the training.
questions.explanation: Simulated phishing tests whether awareness training works by measuring detection, reporting and clicks. The aim is learning, not punishment.

questions.question: What is the first step of the immediate response process for a reported phishing email?
options: Block the sender’s domain
Write the report
Retrieve the original email
Notify the press
questions.hint: You need the real evidence first.
questions.explanation: The order is: retrieve the original email, gather artifacts, notify recipients, analyse artifacts, take defensive measures, then complete the report.

questions.question: Why should analysts work from the original email rather than a forwarded copy?
options: Forwarded emails can’t be opened in any analysis tool
Original emails are always encrypted end to end
Forwarding is faster, so it saves the analyst time
Forwarding can change or strip the headers and attachments needed for analysis
questions.hint: Evidence quality.
questions.explanation: The original from the mail platform, gateway or reporter keeps the headers, body and attachments intact so the investigation is reliable.

questions.question: Which email block is the narrowest?
options: Blocking the single sender address
Blocking the sender’s domain
Blocking the sending server IP
Blocking the whole country
questions.hint: Narrowest affects the fewest legitimate senders.
questions.explanation: Blocking one sender address is narrowest. A domain block is broader, and a sending server IP block is very broad because one IP may serve many senders.

questions.question: A campaign uses many different sender addresses but always the same subject line. Which block helps most?
options: A single sender address block
A subject line block
A DMARC policy change
A WHOIS lookup
questions.hint: Find what stays the same.
questions.explanation: A subject line block catches every message in the campaign even when the attacker rotates sender addresses.

questions.question: Why is blocking a sending server IP considered a strong, high-impact measure?
options: It only ever affects a single email message
It can be undone automatically within an hour
One IP can serve many domains, including legitimate senders
It also blocks the attacker’s phone and laptop
questions.hint: Shared infrastructure.
questions.explanation: A single sending server IP may carry mail for many domains, so blocking it could stop legitimate email too. Justify it carefully.

questions.question: What is the trade-off between a URL block and a domain block?
options: A URL block blocks every site on the server; a domain block blocks one page only
They have exactly the same effect, so the choice doesn’t matter
A domain block only works on email; a URL block only works on the web
A URL block is precise but easy to bypass; a domain block is stronger but may block legitimate access
questions.hint: Precision versus strength.
questions.explanation: A URL block targets one exact address but the attacker can change it. A domain block covers the whole domain and subdomains, with more risk of blocking legitimate business.

questions.question: What is DNS blackholing?
options: Returning a controlled DNS answer so users reach a safe place instead of a malicious site
Removing a malicious domain from the internet so nobody can register it again
Flooding a DNS server with requests until it stops answering anyone at all
Hiding the company’s own DNS records so attackers can’t look them up
questions.hint: The request goes into a ‘hole’.
questions.explanation: DNS blackholing gives a controlled response for a malicious domain, redirecting users to a safe destination instead of the real malicious site.

questions.question: What does a web proxy do?
options: Speeds up email delivery by relaying messages between the company’s mail servers
Sits between users and the internet and allows or denies web requests by policy
Stores a full backup copy of every website staff have visited that week
Signs every outgoing email with the company’s DKIM key before sending
questions.hint: A middleman for web traffic.
questions.explanation: A web proxy sits between users and internet destinations, allowing or denying outbound web requests according to organisational policy.

questions.question: Why is blocking a malicious file by its hash usually better than blocking by file name?
options: File names are always encrypted, so security tools can’t read them
A hash block stops every future version of the malware forever
A hash identifies the exact file; names can be changed or shared by legitimate files
File names only exist on Linux, so name blocks miss Windows files
questions.hint: Renaming a file is easy.
questions.explanation: A hash matches one exact file version, while file names are easy to change and might collide with legitimate files. SHA-256 is the preferred hash to block.

questions.question: Malware changes its code with each version so its hash keeps changing. What is this called?
options: A homoglyph
Macro malware
A lure document
Polymorphic malware
questions.hint: Many forms.
questions.explanation: Polymorphic malware changes its code or representation between versions, which defeats simple hash-based blocking.

questions.question: What is a watchlist used for?
options: Monitoring suspicious indicators and alerting analysts instead of blocking automatically
Automatically blocking every indicator on the list straight away
Listing staff who failed the last phishing simulation
Storing encrypted passwords for privileged accounts
questions.hint: Watch rather than block.
questions.explanation: A watchlist holds suspicious indicators that are monitored rather than blocked. A match raises an alert for an analyst to investigate.

questions.question: What is an IOC?
options: An internal operations committee that approves security changes
An observable artifact linked to malicious activity, like a URL, IP or file hash
A type of email encryption used between mail servers
A firewall rule that blocks traffic from other countries
questions.hint: Indicator of Compromise.
questions.explanation: An Indicator of Compromise is an observable artifact associated with malicious activity, such as a sender address, URL, domain, IP address or file hash.

questions.question: In a report, an analyst writes hxxps://evil[.]com instead of the real link. Why?
options: It’s the encrypted form of the link for safe storage
It’s a shortened URL created for the report
It’s defanged so no one clicks or contacts it by accident
It hides the domain name from the report’s reader
questions.hint: Making dangerous artifacts safe to show.
questions.explanation: Defanging changes URLs and IPs into non-clickable forms, replacing dots with [.] and http/https with hxxp/hxxps, so they can be shared safely.

questions.question: How would 8.8.8.8 be written when defanged?
questions.hint: Brackets around the dots.
questions.explanation: Defanged IP addresses replace each dot with [.], so 8.8.8.8 becomes 8[.]8[.]8[.]8 and can’t be used as a link by accident.

questions.question: What makes a phishing report ‘concise but complete’?
options: Only relevant information, but enough that another analyst needn’t repeat the work
As short as possible, even if some investigation steps are missing
Every log line from the investigation pasted in full
Just the final verdict, with no artifacts or reasoning
questions.hint: Could someone else pick it up?
questions.explanation: Concise means only the relevant information; complete means another analyst can understand the case without re-investigating it.

questions.question: When choosing a defensive measure, what does the course recommend?
options: Always apply the broadest block available, just in case
The narrowest effective control, with the reasoning documented
Avoid blocking anything that might affect the business
Use whichever control is quickest to put in place
questions.hint: Reduce risk without stopping the business.
questions.explanation: Pick the narrowest control that effectively reduces risk without unnecessarily disrupting legitimate business, and document the justification.

questions.question: What is the purpose of an audit trail in an investigation?
options: A list of staff who reported phishing
A log of the attacker’s own actions only
A traceable record of what was found, analysed and changed
A backup of all deleted emails
questions.hint: Accountability.
questions.explanation: An audit trail records what was identified, analysed and changed, supporting accountability and later review.

questions.question: What is email triage?
options: Automatically deleting all spam before it reaches inboxes
Encrypting suspicious emails so they can be stored safely
Writing the final investigation report for management
The first assessment to decide if an email is legitimate, spam, suspicious or malicious
questions.hint: Sorting before the deep dive.
questions.explanation: Email triage is the initial assessment that classifies a reported email and decides how much investigation it needs.

questions.question: An attachment is called invoice.pdf.exe. What type of file is it?
options: An executable
A PDF document
A compressed archive
A web page
questions.hint: Read the final extension.
questions.explanation: This is a double extension. The last extension decides the real type, so invoice.pdf.exe is an executable disguised as a PDF.

questions.question: What does an email gateway do when it performs attachment stripping?
options: Compresses attachments so emails take up less space
Removes a dangerous attachment before delivery, sometimes leaving a notice
Adds a digital signature to every attachment
Converts attachments into Base64 for safe delivery
questions.hint: The attachment never arrives.
questions.explanation: Attachment stripping removes suspicious or malicious attachments at the gateway before delivery, often replacing them with a notice.

questions.question: An email’s display name says ‘IT Service Desk’. What should an analyst check?
options: Nothing more: display names are verified by the server
Only the subject line and the time it was sent
The real sending address and supporting header evidence
Whether the email contains the company logo
questions.hint: The friendly name can be set to anything.
questions.explanation: Display names can say anything. Verify the actual address and headers, such as the sending server and authentication results.

questions.question: Suspicious appearance alone is enough to classify an email as malicious. True or false?
options: True: any email that looks odd should be treated as malicious
True, but only if the email contains an attachment
False: only the person who received it can decide
False: classify on intent, artifacts and analysis evidence
questions.hint: Evidence, not looks.
questions.explanation: Odd formatting doesn’t prove malice. Classify based on intent, artifacts and the results of analysis.

questions.question: What is the end-to-end phishing workflow taught in the course?
options: Triage, collect artifacts, analyse, defend, report
Report, defend, analyse, collect, triage
Block, delete, forget
Analyse, report, then triage
questions.hint: Classify first, report last.
questions.explanation: The workflow is: triage and classify, collect artifacts, analyse them, choose defensive measures, then report the findings.

questions.question: What are Microsoft ASR rules used for?
options: Checking whether a domain’s SPF record is valid
Restricting risky behaviour, like Office apps creating executable content
Sending simulated phishing emails to employees
Defanging URLs automatically in incident reports
questions.hint: Attack Surface Reduction.
questions.explanation: Attack Surface Reduction rules block risky behaviours, such as Office applications creating executables, to reduce chances for malware to run.

questions.question: Attackers copy the Outlook on the web sign-in page to steal work passwords. What is this page usually called in the course?
options: A DMARC report
A mail relay
A fake OWA login portal
A tracking pixel
questions.hint: OWA is Outlook’s web access.
questions.explanation: OWA (Outlook Web Access) login pages are frequently imitated in credential-harvesting campaigns.

questions.question: What is a lure email?
options: A bounce message sent back by a mail server when an address doesn’t exist
An email that has passed SPF and DKIM checks and been signed by the sender
A marketing newsletter the user subscribed to and has since forgotten about
The first deceptive email that persuades the victim to click, open or enter details
questions.hint: It’s the bait.
questions.explanation: A lure email is the initial deceptive message designed to get the recipient to take the attacker’s desired action.

questions.question: What is a mail relay?
options: An intermediary server that forwards email towards its destination
A tool that decodes Base64 in email bodies
A type of spam filter that learns from users
A web page used to read email in a browser
questions.hint: Passing the message along.
questions.explanation: A mail relay is an intermediary mail server that forwards email towards another server or its final destination.

questions.question: What is an MTA?
options: A Malware Threat Alert raised by antivirus
A Mail Transfer Agent that moves email between servers
A Message Tracking Archive kept for audits
A Managed Trust Authority that signs certificates
questions.hint: Like a mail-sorting office.
questions.explanation: A Mail Transfer Agent transports email between servers, a bit like a sorting office passing post along.

questions.question: What is the difference between a threat feed and a one-off reputation search?
options: A feed checks one file at a time; a search covers every known indicator
They are identical: both are updated continuously in the background
A feed supplies regularly updated bad indicators; a one-off search checks one artifact now
A search runs automatically; a feed has to be checked by hand each time
questions.hint: Continuous versus at that moment.
questions.explanation: A threat feed keeps supplying updated known-bad indicators for proactive blocking. A one-off reputation search checks a single artifact at investigation time.

questions.question: Which Cisco service checks a file’s SHA-256 hash against its reputation database?
options: PhishTank
URLhaus
WHOIS
Talos File Reputation
questions.hint: Cisco’s intelligence team is called Talos.
questions.explanation: Talos File Reputation checks SHA-256 hashes against the Talos database and returns a reputation result plus file metadata.

questions.question: A sandbox report maps the malware’s behaviour to tactics and techniques. Which framework is it most likely using?
options: MITRE ATT&CK
The CIA triad
The OSI model
DMARC
questions.hint: A framework describing adversary behaviour.
questions.explanation: MITRE ATT&CK describes adversary behaviour as tactics and techniques, and sandbox reports often map observed activity to it.

questions.question: What does a recon email that bounces back tell the attacker?
options: That the user clicked the link
That the mailbox probably doesn’t exist
That the user’s password is weak
That SPF is misconfigured
questions.hint: Undeliverable means…
questions.explanation: A bounce (undeliverable message) suggests the mailbox doesn’t exist. No bounce suggests it does, making it a future target.

questions.question: What should a phishing investigation report include?
options: Only the attacker’s name and where they are based
Just the total number of emails that were received
Email description, artifacts, analysis, defensive actions and lessons learned
The affected users’ passwords so they can be reset
questions.hint: Enough to understand and act on the case.
questions.explanation: A good report covers what the email looked like, the artifacts or IOCs, the analysis and results, the defensive measures taken, and lessons learned.

questions.question: What is the main job of a SIEM?
options: Encrypting data stored on company servers and backups
Blocking malicious websites before staff can visit them
Managing staff passwords and multi-factor sign-in
Centralising and analysing activity from many systems to detect and investigate threats
questions.hint: One place to see everything.
questions.explanation: A SIEM collects, stores, normalises and analyses activity from many sources so the security team can detect threats, investigate and respond from one place.

questions.question: SIEM is a combination of which two older ideas?
options: SIM and SEM
SOC and SOAR
IDS and IPS
EDR and NDR
questions.hint: Information management plus event management.
questions.explanation: SIEM combines Security Information Management (collecting, storing and reporting) with Security Event Management (real-time monitoring, correlation and alerting).

questions.question: Which side of SIEM focuses on real-time monitoring, correlation and alerting?
options: SIM
SEM
SOAR
UEBA
questions.hint: E for event.
questions.explanation: Security Event Management handles the live side: monitoring events, correlating them and alerting. SIM handles longer-term collection, storage and reporting.

questions.question: Which side of SIEM focuses on collecting, storing and reporting on security information?
options: SEM
NDR
SIM
EDR
questions.hint: I for information.
questions.explanation: Security Information Management covers collecting, storing, translating, analysing and reporting security information from many sources.

questions.question: What is the difference between an event and an alert?
options: An event is always malicious; an alert is always harmless activity
They are two words for the same thing in a SIEM
An alert is recorded activity; an event is the notification sent
An event is recorded activity; an alert is raised when logic flags activity needing attention
questions.hint: Not every event deserves attention.
questions.explanation: An event is anything recorded, such as a login or process start. An alert is a notification created when detection logic finds activity that needs an analyst.

questions.question: Which of these is a log source for a SIEM?
options: A firewall
A dashboard panel
A correlation rule
A Sigma condition
questions.hint: Something that generates logs.
questions.explanation: Log sources generate the data: firewalls, servers, domain controllers, proxies, IDS/IPS, antivirus and EDR. Dashboards and rules work on that data.

questions.question: A SIEM brings logs from hundreds of systems into one platform. What is this step called?
options: Normalisation
Aggregation
Correlation
Enrichment
questions.hint: Bringing it all together.
questions.explanation: Aggregation combines logs from many sources into a central platform. Normalisation then makes the fields consistent, and correlation connects related events.

questions.question: One firewall logs ‘src_ip’ and another logs ‘SourceAddress’. Which SIEM step makes these consistent?
options: Aggregation
Correlation
Normalisation
Retention
questions.hint: Making the formats the same.
questions.explanation: Normalisation converts differently formatted logs into consistent fields, so events from different products can be compared and correlated.

questions.question: Failed logins on a VPN, then a successful login, then a large download: linking these events is called what?
options: Aggregation
Normalisation
Indexing
Correlation
questions.hint: Connecting the dots across sources.
questions.explanation: Correlation links events from one or more sources to reveal patterns, like a brute-force attempt followed by data theft.

questions.question: Which SIEM component applies rules and analytics to incoming data to find activity of interest?
options: The correlation engine
The front-end dashboard
The log collector
The SIEM database
questions.hint: The ‘brain’ of the SIEM.
questions.explanation: The correlation engine evaluates incoming data using rules, analytics or statistics to identify suspicious activity.

questions.question: A SIEM alerts on a legitimate admin running a scheduled backup. What is this?
options: A false negative
A false positive
A true positive
A true negative
questions.hint: Harmless activity flagged as bad.
questions.explanation: A false positive is benign activity alerted as malicious. Too many of them cause alert fatigue, so rules are tuned to reduce them.

questions.question: An attacker’s activity goes completely unnoticed by the SIEM. What is this?
options: A false positive
A true positive
A false negative
A policy violation
questions.hint: Malicious, but missed.
questions.explanation: A false negative is malicious activity that isn’t detected. Tuning must reduce false positives without creating false negatives.

questions.question: Why do SIEMs keep historical logs?
options: Because older logs are needed to generate new alerts
To replace the need for backups of company data
Because logs can’t be deleted once they are created
So analysts can investigate earlier activity and build timelines
questions.hint: Looking back after something’s found.
questions.explanation: Retained historical logs let analysts investigate past activity, reconstruct timelines and support forensic investigations and audits.

questions.question: What is the difference between a SaaS SIEM and an on-premises SIEM?
options: SaaS is hosted by the vendor; on-premises runs on the organisation’s own infrastructure
SaaS only collects cloud logs; on-premises only collects office logs
On-premises is always cheaper and needs no administration
They differ only in their licence, not where they run
questions.hint: Who hosts it?
questions.explanation: A SaaS SIEM is delivered as a hosted service with the vendor providing infrastructure. An on-premises SIEM runs inside the organisation, which must provide compute, storage and administration.

questions.question: How does SOAR differ from SIEM?
options: SOAR collects logs; SIEM automates the response to alerts
SOAR orchestrates tools and automates response; SIEM focuses on visibility and alerts
SOAR is a type of firewall; SIEM is a type of antivirus
They are the same product sold under different names
questions.hint: Orchestration, automation and response.
questions.explanation: SIEM centralises data, correlates and alerts. SOAR coordinates security tools and automates repeatable response workflows, often triggered by SIEM alerts.

questions.question: Which technology models normal user behaviour and flags deviations, like a user suddenly downloading gigabytes at 3am?
options: SOAR
Syslog
UEBA
NetFlow
questions.hint: Behaviour analytics.
questions.explanation: User and Entity Behaviour Analytics learns normal behaviour for users and devices and flags anomalies that may be malicious or risky.

questions.question: What does NDR focus on?
options: Detecting threats on individual laptops and servers
Automating responses across many security tools
Storing logs for compliance reporting
Detecting and responding to threats using network traffic
questions.hint: Network Detection and Response.
questions.explanation: NDR detects and responds to suspicious activity using network telemetry, whereas EDR focuses on endpoints and SIEM on centralised correlation.

questions.question: Adding the country an IP address belongs to, or a threat-intel verdict, to an alert is called what?
options: Enrichment
Normalisation
Aggregation
Parsing
questions.hint: Adding context.
questions.explanation: Enrichment adds contextual information, such as geolocation or threat intelligence, to make alerts quicker to understand and prioritise.

questions.question: What is incident triage in a SOC?
options: Writing the final report once an incident is closed
Quickly assessing an alert to decide its priority and next steps
Deleting low-priority alerts without looking at them
Restoring systems from backups after an attack
questions.hint: Sorting by urgency.
questions.explanation: Triage is a rapid assessment of an alert or event to judge its significance, priority and what should happen next.

questions.question: An auditor asks for proof that admin logins are monitored. Which SIEM use case helps?
options: Event streaming
DNS tunnelling detection
Compliance reporting
Packet capture
questions.hint: Proving requirements are met.
questions.explanation: Compliance reporting uses centralised log data to show that security and regulatory requirements, like monitoring admin access, are being met.

questions.question: Why should logging be scoped rather than sending everything to the SIEM?
options: Because SIEMs can only accept logs from ten sources
Because logs from servers are never useful for security
To make sure no alerts are ever generated
To keep useful visibility without unnecessary noise and cost
questions.hint: A SIEM isn’t just a log dump.
questions.explanation: Log scoping selects the systems and event types worth sending, keeping the visibility you need without drowning analysts in noise or paying to store junk.

questions.question: What is Syslog?
options: A standard protocol for sending log messages to a central server
A Windows tool for viewing event logs
A query language for searching Azure logs
A file format for captured network packets
questions.hint: Defined in RFC 5424.
questions.explanation: Syslog is the standard protocol for sending event and system log messages from devices to a central Syslog server.

questions.question: What is the default transport and port for Syslog?
options: TCP 443
UDP 514
UDP 53
TCP 3389
questions.hint: Fast, but with no delivery guarantee.
questions.explanation: Syslog defaults to UDP port 514, which is lightweight but doesn’t guarantee delivery. TCP 514 is more reliable, and TCP 6514 is commonly used for secure Syslog.

questions.question: Which port is commonly used for securely transported Syslog?
options: UDP 514
TCP 25
TCP 6514
UDP 161
questions.hint: It’s a higher number than the default.
questions.explanation: TCP 6514 is commonly used for Syslog sent over a secure, encrypted transport. UDP 514 is the unencrypted default.

questions.question: How is a Syslog PRI value calculated?
options: Facility code + severity + 8
Severity × facility code
(Severity × 8) − facility code
(Facility code × 8) + severity
questions.hint: Facility is multiplied first.
questions.explanation: The priority value combines facility and severity: PRI = (facility × 8) + severity. It sits at the start of a Syslog message, before the header.

questions.question: What are the three parts of a Syslog message?
options: PRI, header and message
Source, destination and port
Index, sourcetype and host
Logsource, detection and condition
questions.hint: Priority first.
questions.explanation: A Syslog message has the PRI (priority), a header (timestamp, hostname, app) and the message content itself.

questions.question: In which file format are modern Windows event logs stored?
options: .pcap
.evtx
.eml
.json
questions.hint: EV for event.
questions.explanation: Windows Event Logs are stored in the binary .evtx format and can be viewed and filtered in Event Viewer.

questions.question: Which Windows Event ID records a successful logon?
questions.hint: One of the most-searched IDs.
questions.explanation: 4624 is a successful logon. 4634 is a logoff, 4720 is a new user account and 4732 is a member added to a local security group.

questions.question: Which Windows Event ID shows a logon that was given special or administrative privileges?
questions.hint: ‘Special logon’.
questions.explanation: 4672 is a special logon: the session received admin-level privileges. It’s often seen alongside 4624 for privileged accounts.

questions.question: An analyst suspects an attacker created a backdoor account. Which Event ID should they search for?
questions.hint: A new user account.
questions.explanation: Event ID 4720 is generated when a user account is created, which makes it key for spotting attackers adding their own accounts.

questions.question: Which Windows Event ID shows a member being added to a security-enabled local group, such as Administrators?
questions.hint: Group membership change.
questions.explanation: 4732 records a member added to a security-enabled local group, a common step when attackers give themselves admin rights.

questions.question: What is the difference between Event IDs 4647 and 4634?
options: 4647 is a failed logon; 4634 is a successful logon
4647 is account creation; 4634 is account deletion
4647 is a user-initiated logoff; 4634 shows a logon session ended
They both record new processes starting
questions.hint: Both are about logging off.
questions.explanation: 4647 is logged when a user starts the logoff, and 4634 records that a logon session has ended.

questions.question: What does Sysmon add to Windows logging?
options: Encryption of Windows event logs so attackers can’t read or alter them
A full replacement for antivirus that removes malware it finds
Automatic blocking of any process that isn’t digitally signed
Richer endpoint detail, such as full command lines, parent processes and hashes
questions.hint: It’s a Sysinternals monitoring tool.
questions.explanation: Sysmon records detailed endpoint activity to the event log: process creation with command lines and parents, network connections, hashes, drivers and DLLs.

questions.question: Why does Sysmon log changes to a file’s creation time?
options: Malware may change timestamps to hide when it arrived
It’s needed to calculate the file’s hash
Windows requires it for every file
It shows who owns the file
questions.hint: Timestomping.
questions.explanation: Attackers can change file creation times to blend in. Sysmon logging those changes helps investigators spot the tampering.

questions.question: Why do analysts tune a Sysmon configuration?
options: To make Sysmon run faster than antivirus
To keep useful telemetry while filtering out noisy events
To stop Sysmon logging process creation
To encrypt the events it records
questions.hint: Signal versus noise.
questions.explanation: A Sysmon configuration includes and excludes events so you keep valuable endpoint data without flooding the SIEM with noise.

questions.question: Which query language is used to search logs in Microsoft Azure monitoring services?
options: SQL
SPL
KQL
YAML
questions.hint: Kusto.
questions.explanation: Kusto Query Language (KQL) is used to search and analyse logs in Azure Monitor and Log Analytics workspaces.

questions.question: Where does Azure store monitoring data so it can be queried?
options: An Event Viewer custom view
A Splunk index
A Syslog server
A Log Analytics workspace
questions.hint: Azure’s own log store.
questions.explanation: Azure Monitor sends data to a Log Analytics workspace, where it can be stored and queried with KQL.

questions.question: Cloud services commonly expose log data through which kind of interface?
options: A REST API returning JSON
A Syslog feed over UDP 514
Printed daily reports
A PCAP file per day
questions.hint: HTTP-based, structured text.
questions.explanation: Cloud platforms usually expose data through HTTP-based REST APIs, often in JSON format, which SIEMs collect directly.

questions.question: What does osquery let analysts do?
options: Capture and index full network traffic
Query an endpoint’s operating system state using SQL
Convert Sigma rules into SIEM queries
Decode Base64 in suspicious emails
questions.hint: The OS as database tables.
questions.explanation: osquery exposes operating system information as relational tables that can be queried with SQL, giving consistent endpoint visibility.

questions.question: What does Arkime (formerly Moloch) do?
options: Queries endpoint state using SQL tables
Converts Sigma rules for different SIEMs
Stores and indexes network traffic as PCAP for fast searching
Scans websites for known vulnerabilities
questions.hint: Network packet capture at scale.
questions.explanation: Arkime captures and indexes network traffic in standard PCAP format, so analysts can search, browse and export sessions quickly.

questions.question: What is a PCAP file?
options: A binary Windows event log viewed in Event Viewer
A compressed bundle of Sigma rules for sharing
A feed of known malicious IP addresses and domains
A file of captured network traffic for later analysis
questions.hint: Packet capture.
questions.explanation: PCAP files contain captured network packets that can be analysed later in tools like Wireshark or Arkime.

questions.question: Which of these are examples of event streaming from network devices?
options: SNMP, NetFlow and IPFIX
SPF, DKIM and DMARC
KQL, SQL and SPL
MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-256
questions.hint: Protocols that stream device and flow data.
questions.explanation: Event streaming uses protocols like SNMP, NetFlow and IPFIX to push operational and flow information from network devices to a collector.

questions.question: What is the difference between structured and unstructured log data?
options: Structured is encrypted; unstructured is in plain text
Structured has consistent fields; unstructured needs more parsing first
Unstructured is always more accurate than structured
Structured logs only come from cloud services
questions.hint: Predictable fields or not.
questions.explanation: Structured logs have clearly defined, predictable fields and are easy to normalise. Unstructured logs lack consistent fields and need more parsing.

questions.question: What does parsing do to a raw log message?
options: Encrypts the message so it can be stored safely
Deletes duplicate log messages from storage
Extracts fields and values so the data can be searched and normalised
Sends the message on to a Syslog server
questions.hint: Pulling the fields out.
questions.explanation: Parsing extracts fields and values from raw logs. Indexing then makes them fast to search, and normalisation maps them to common names.

questions.question: What is a log collector?
options: A dashboard that shows log volumes over time
A person who reviews logs by hand each day
A rule that deletes old logs after a set time
An agent or service that captures logs and forwards them to a central SIEM
questions.hint: It gathers and forwards.
questions.explanation: A log collector captures logs, may parse them, and forwards them to an aggregator or SIEM. The source generates events; the aggregator centralises them.

questions.question: What does categorisation add to normalised events?
options: Meaning, by grouping events into types like authentication or remote access
External context, such as threat-intel verdicts and IP geolocation
Encryption of each event so it meets compliance requirements
Faster searching by organising stored data into indexes
questions.hint: Labelling what kind of event it is.
questions.explanation: Categorisation classifies events into meaningful groups, such as authentication or system activity. Enrichment adds external context; normalisation standardises fields.

questions.question: What is the difference between an out-of-the-box rule and a custom detection rule?
options: Custom rules are written by the vendor; out-of-the-box rules by analysts
Vendor rules give generic coverage; custom rules fit your environment and threats
Out-of-the-box rules never produce false positives
Custom rules can’t raise alerts, only reports
questions.hint: Who wrote it, and for whom?
questions.explanation: Out-of-the-box rules are prebuilt by the SIEM vendor for common attacks. Custom rules are written for your organisation’s systems, behaviour and threats.

questions.question: What is the difference between a real-time rule and a scheduled rule?
options: Scheduled rules are always more accurate than real-time rules
Real-time rules only run overnight
Real-time rules evaluate continuously; scheduled rules run at set intervals
There is no difference in how they run
questions.hint: Always on versus every so often.
questions.explanation: Real-time rules evaluate events as they arrive. Scheduled rules run periodically, such as every few minutes or daily.

questions.question: A rule only alerts after 10 failed logons from the same IP within five minutes. What is this called?
options: A rule exclusion
Normalisation
Enrichment
A rule threshold
questions.hint: A minimum amount before alerting.
questions.explanation: A threshold requires a number or rate of matching events before alerting, cutting noise from the odd mistyped password.

questions.question: A network-scan detection keeps firing on the company’s approved vulnerability scanner. What is the best fix?
options: Add an exclusion for the scanner’s IP while keeping its logs
Delete the detection rule so it can never fire again
Stop collecting network logs from that part of the site
Raise the rule’s severity so analysts look at it faster
questions.hint: Ignore known-good, keep visibility.
questions.explanation: A rule exclusion deliberately ignores known benign activity, like an approved scanner, while the telemetry stays available for investigation.

questions.question: What is the goal of rule tuning?
options: Make every rule trigger as often as possible
Reduce false positives without creating false negatives
Remove all rules that ever fire
Speed up log collection from sources
questions.hint: Balance noise and misses.
questions.explanation: Tuning adjusts logic, thresholds and exclusions so detections stay useful, cutting unnecessary alerts without missing real attacks.

questions.question: What is Sigma?
options: A commercial SIEM platform made by IBM for large SOCs
A Sysinternals service that logs detailed endpoint activity
A vendor-agnostic, shareable format for writing detection rules
A query language used to search Azure Log Analytics data
questions.hint: Write once, convert for many SIEMs.
questions.explanation: Sigma is a generic, human-readable rule format for log-based detections that can be converted into queries for supported SIEM platforms.

questions.question: What problem does Sigma help organisations avoid?
options: Running out of log storage
Needing any log sources at all
Writing incident reports
Vendor lock-in to one SIEM’s rule format
questions.hint: Moving detections between platforms.
questions.explanation: Because Sigma rules are vendor-agnostic, detections can be shared and converted for other SIEMs, reducing dependence on one vendor.

questions.question: Which part of a Sigma rule states what kind of logs the detection needs, such as Windows process creation?
options: The logsource
The condition
The level
The tags
questions.hint: Where the data comes from.
questions.explanation: The logsource section identifies the telemetry needed. The detection section defines the selections, and the condition decides when they count as a match.

questions.question: In a Sigma rule, what does the ‘falsepositives’ field describe?
options: Real attacks the rule has previously failed to detect
Known legitimate situations that could trigger the rule
The severity level given to alerts the rule raises
The SIEM platforms the rule can be converted for
questions.hint: Expected benign triggers.
questions.explanation: The falsepositives field lists legitimate scenarios that might trigger the detection, helping analysts judge alerts quickly.

questions.question: What does Sigmac do?
options: Collects Windows logs from domain controllers
Encrypts Sigma rules before sharing them
Converts Sigma rules into queries for specific SIEM platforms
Scores Sigma rules for accuracy
questions.hint: Sigma converter.
questions.explanation: Sigmac translates Sigma rules into SIEM-specific query or rule formats for supported platforms.

questions.question: What do Sigma tags commonly link a rule to?
options: The analyst who wrote the rule
The licence the SIEM runs under
Specific users who triggered it
MITRE ATT&CK tactics or techniques
questions.hint: A well-known framework of attacker behaviour.
questions.explanation: Sigma tags usually reference MITRE ATT&CK tactic or technique IDs, so detections can be mapped to known adversary behaviour.

questions.question: Unusually long or frequent DNS queries to one domain could indicate which technique?
options: DNS tunnelling
Typosquatting
Credential stuffing
Smishing
questions.hint: Data hidden inside DNS.
questions.explanation: DNS tunnelling abuses DNS queries and responses to carry data or command-and-control traffic. Unusual query patterns or volume can reveal it.

questions.question: MITRE ATT&CK T1071.004 covers adversaries using which protocol for command and control?
options: SMTP
DNS
FTP
SNMP
questions.hint: Application Layer Protocol: …
questions.explanation: T1071.004 is Application Layer Protocol: DNS, covering attackers who use DNS for command-and-control communication.

questions.question: In Splunk, what is the difference between an index and a sourcetype?
options: A sourcetype is where data is stored; an index describes the format of each event
They are two names for the same thing, used in different Splunk versions
An index is the stored collection of data; sourcetype is the format of events within it
An index is a type of dashboard; a sourcetype is a type of saved report
questions.hint: Container versus type.
questions.explanation: An index is a named collection of stored data. Sourcetype identifies the format or type of event, such as Suricata or Windows events.

questions.question: In Splunk, what does the ‘host’ field identify?
options: The format of the event data
The file the data came from
The analyst running the search
The system the event is associated with
questions.hint: Which machine?
questions.explanation: host is the system associated with the event. source is where the data came from, and sourcetype is the event format.

questions.question: A Splunk search uses dest_ip="10.10.10.*". What does the asterisk do?
options: Acts as a wildcard matching any value in that position
Excludes those addresses from the results
Marks the field as required
Sorts the results by IP address
questions.hint: Broadening the match.
questions.explanation: The asterisk is a wildcard, matching any characters in that position, so this matches every address in 10.10.10.x.

questions.question: In a Splunk search, what does the pipe character (|) do?
options: Comments out everything after it in the search bar
Passes results from one command to the next in a pipeline
Combines two separate indexes into a single one
Separates a field name from the value being searched
questions.hint: Chaining commands.
questions.explanation: The pipe joins commands into a pipeline, with each command processing the results of the previous one.

questions.question: Which Splunk command calculates summaries, such as a count of events per IP address?
options: table
sort
stats
dedup
questions.hint: Statistics.
questions.explanation: stats calculates statistics like counts grouped by a field. table shows chosen fields, sort orders results and dedup removes duplicates.

questions.question: Which Splunk command shows only the fields you choose, in a table?
options: stats
spath
sort
table
questions.hint: Its name says it.
questions.explanation: table displays only the selected fields, cutting noise so results are easier to review.

questions.question: Which Splunk command removes duplicate results based on a field?
options: dedup
stats
table
sort
questions.hint: De-duplicate.
questions.explanation: dedup removes duplicate results based on one or more fields, a practical way to list unique values.

questions.question: Which Splunk command orders results, for example to rebuild a sequence of events?
options: dedup
sort
values
spath
questions.hint: Ascending or descending.
questions.explanation: sort orders results by a field, ascending or descending, which is useful for reconstructing what happened when.

questions.question: In Sysmon events, which two fields are most useful for seeing what a process actually ran?
options: host and source
Logon ID and Session GUID
Image and CommandLine
Facility and severity
questions.hint: The executable path and its arguments.
questions.explanation: Image shows the executable’s path and CommandLine shows the arguments it ran with, which together reveal what a process actually did.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Splunk alert trigger and an alert action?
options: The action decides when it fires; the trigger sends the email
They are the same setting shown twice
Triggers are only for dashboards, actions only for reports
The trigger is when it fires; the action is what Splunk does next
questions.hint: When versus what.
questions.explanation: The trigger is the condition for the alert to fire, such as a threshold. The action is what happens afterwards, like a notification or log entry.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Splunk report and a dashboard panel?
options: A report is a saved search; a panel visualises data powered by a search or report
A panel is a saved search; a report is a chart that sits on a dashboard
Reports can only be run once, while panels can be reused anywhere
They are the same feature, just shown in different parts of Splunk
questions.hint: Saved search versus visual.
questions.explanation: A report is a reusable saved search. A dashboard panel displays data as a table, chart or counter, powered by a search or report.

questions.question: What does ‘single pane of glass’ mean in a SOC?
options: A one-way mirror in the security operations room
One consolidated view of the key security metrics and visuals
A single analyst watching every alert
Using only one log source for simplicity
questions.hint: Everything on one screen.
questions.explanation: A single pane of glass puts the most important security information on one screen for fast situational awareness.

questions.question: An analyst finds a suspicious IP in firewall logs, then searches the proxy and endpoint logs for it. What is this called?
options: Log scoping
Event sampling
Log source pivoting
Normalisation
questions.hint: Using one clue to search elsewhere.
questions.explanation: Pivoting uses an indicator from one source, like an IP or hash, to find more context in other sources.

questions.question: Why must analysts watch for field-name variance when pivoting between products?
options: Field names change every time the SIEM restarts
Different products can’t log the same information
Field names are encrypted in some log sources
The same idea may be called src_ip in one product and SourceIp in another
questions.hint: Same meaning, different labels.
questions.explanation: Products name the same concept differently, so analysts search by meaning rather than assuming identical field names.

questions.question: Why might an analyst use event sampling (such as 1:100) in Splunk?
options: To explore data quickly before running the full search
To permanently delete 99% of the events
To make alerts fire 100 times faster
To encrypt the search results
questions.hint: A quick look first.
questions.explanation: Sampling searches a fraction of events to speed up exploration. The final query is then rerun without sampling for complete results.

questions.question: Does a SIEM replace the need for analysts?
options: Yes: SIEMs investigate and close every alert
No: tuning and human investigation are still needed
Yes, but only for small organisations
No: SIEMs can’t raise alerts without analysts
questions.hint: Tools support people.
questions.explanation: A SIEM surfaces and correlates activity, but rules need tuning and alerts still need human judgement and investigation.

questions.question: What is the typical order of the core SIEM flow?
options: Alerts, correlation, normalisation, collection, log sources
Storage, alerts, log sources, collection
Log sources, collection, normalisation, correlation, storage, alerts
Correlation, log sources, alerts, normalisation
questions.hint: Data in, alerts out.
questions.explanation: Logs come from sources, are collected and aggregated, normalised, correlated and stored, then surface as alerts and dashboards.

questions.question: What is detection engineering?
options: Physically installing sensors in a data centre
Engineering networks to avoid detection
Writing marketing material for a SIEM product
Designing, testing and tuning detection logic over time
questions.hint: Building and maintaining detections.
questions.explanation: Detection engineering is the discipline of designing, testing, tuning and maintaining detection logic based on available telemetry.

questions.question: Searching the SIEM for a known-malicious hash to find every affected host is an example of what?
options: An IOC search
Log scoping
Normalisation
Rule tuning
questions.hint: Indicators of Compromise.
questions.explanation: An IOC search queries collected data for indicators like hashes, IPs or domains to identify affected users and hosts.

questions.question: What does indexing do for log data?
options: Encrypts it for long-term storage
Organises it so large datasets can be searched quickly
Converts it into a consistent field format
Deletes logs that are older than a year
questions.hint: Like the index in a book.
questions.explanation: Indexing organises ingested data for fast searching. Normalisation is the separate step that makes field names consistent.

questions.question: What does Splunk’s values() function return when used with stats?
options: The number of events in an index
The average of a numeric field
The distinct values of a field
The first event in the results
questions.hint: Unique values, grouped.
questions.explanation: values() returns the distinct values of a field, useful for summarising, for example, every command line run on each host.

questions.question: What is the difference between a scheduled alert and a real-time alert in Splunk?
options: Real-time alerts run once a day; scheduled alerts run continuously
Scheduled alerts can’t trigger actions, only appear on dashboards
There’s no difference; the names describe the same type of alert
Scheduled alerts run at intervals; real-time alerts evaluate continuously
questions.hint: Same idea as rules.
questions.explanation: A scheduled alert runs its search at defined intervals. A real-time alert evaluates activity continuously within a time window.

questions.question: In Event Viewer, what is a Custom View?
options: A saved filter for chosen logs, IDs, users or time ranges
A theme that changes Event Viewer’s colours
A way to delete events in bulk
A tool that converts .evtx to PCAP
questions.hint: Filtering the noise.
questions.explanation: A Custom View saves a filter so analysts can focus on selected logs, event levels, IDs, keywords, users, computers or times.

questions.question: Which Windows log records logons, account management and privilege use under the audit policy?
options: The Application event log
The Security event log
The Setup event log
The DNS server log
questions.hint: Security-relevant activity.
questions.explanation: The Security event log holds events generated by Windows security audit policies, including logons, account changes and privilege use.

questions.question: What does the Windows Logon ID help analysts do?
options: Identify which user created a file
Calculate a file’s hash
Link together events from the same logon session
Find the IP address of a website
questions.hint: It ties a session together.
questions.explanation: The Logon ID is a semi-unique identifier that links events belonging to the same Windows logon session.

questions.question: Event ID 5379 appears on a workstation. What does it indicate?
options: A new local user account was just created
A user started logging off from their session
A member was added to a local security group
Stored Credential Manager credentials were read
questions.hint: Saved credentials.
questions.explanation: 5379 means credentials stored in Credential Manager were read, which can be worth investigating if unexpected.

questions.question: Which SIEM platform is made by IBM and can use X-Force threat intelligence?
options: QRadar
Graylog
Arkime
Splunk
questions.hint: IBM’s SIEM.
questions.explanation: QRadar is IBM’s SIEM platform, and it can use IBM X-Force threat intelligence to enrich investigations.

questions.question: Which log management and SIEM platform comes in both open-source and commercial editions?
options: QRadar
Graylog
ArcSight ESM
Azure Monitor
questions.hint: One of these has a free version.
questions.explanation: Graylog is a log management and SIEM platform with open-source and commercial editions.

questions.question: A SIEM is used to check that a ‘no USB storage’ policy is actually being followed. What is this called?
options: Log source pivoting
Rule threshold tuning
Policy enforcement validation
Event streaming analysis
questions.hint: Proving controls work.
questions.explanation: Policy enforcement validation uses logs to verify security policies and controls are operating as intended.

questions.question: What is real-time monitoring?
options: Reviewing the previous month’s logs together at the end of each quarter
Recording CCTV footage of the server room so access can be checked
Running a vulnerability scan across the network once every week
Continuously analysing incoming events so suspicious activity is spotted quickly
questions.hint: As it happens.
questions.explanation: Real-time monitoring continuously observes and analyses incoming events so suspicious activity can be identified fast.

questions.question: What makes information ‘actionable’ for a SOC analyst?
options: It has enough context and relevance to support a useful action
It has been encrypted before being shared with the team
It comes from a paid commercial threat-intelligence feed
It has been approved by a manager before it is used
questions.hint: Can you do something with it?
questions.explanation: Actionable information has enough context and relevance for an analyst or automated system to take a useful security action.
